_format: Projects a maintainer has looked at and decided not to list.
scripts/find-candidates.js reads this file every run and subtracts it from
the search results, so anything here is never proposed again. Without it a
rejected project comes back next month and the month after, and by the
third identical report everybody has muted the issue. That is why this is
committed to the repository rather than kept in workflow state.
Each element of "declined" is an object:
url    (required) the repository or project URL, as it appeared in the
report. Matched after normalization, so http vs https, a trailing
slash, and a www. prefix are all the same entry.
reason (required) why it was declined, in a sentence. Required on
purpose: a decline with no reason cannot be revisited later, and
a run refuses to start if one is missing.
date   (conventional) ISO date of the decision, so a decline made under
old circumstances can be found and reconsidered.
To decline a candidate: copy its Repository URL out of the discovery issue,
add an object here, and commit. To un-decline one, delete its object.

declined.reason: This list itself. It matches most of the search terms and would otherwise be proposed for inclusion in itself.
Bootable USB creator for installing operating systems. Carries the secure-boot topic, but it is not an embedded security tool.
USB drive formatting and bootable media utility. Same reason as Ventoy: the secure-boot topic is incidental to what it does.
Android app for viewing Apple FindMy trackers. A consumer utility rather than embedded security tooling.
Secure Boot key manager for desktop Linux UEFI. Good at its job, but the target is general-purpose machines, not embedded devices.
Secure Boot and measured boot for NixOS on desktop and server Linux. Out of scope for the same reason as sbctl.

IoT PKI library whose scope is hard to judge: the repository is recent and its description reads as a feature list rather than a statement of what it does. Worth reconsidering if it establishes a track record.
Service mesh for Kubernetes. Carries the fault-injection topic, but there it means chaos testing of network calls, not glitching a chip.
Index of general electronics and mechanical engineering YouTube channels. Not a security resource.

Flying-probe automation for hardware hacking, and the idea is in scope, but there is nothing here to evaluate: two commits, both on the day the repository was created, one contributor, no license, and one watcher against 331 stars and 20 forks. Worth reconsidering if real development follows.

General-purpose AI pentesting platform spanning web, cloud, identity, CI/CD, Active Directory and Kubernetes; IoT firmware is one target among many rather than its subject. The description is also promotional in a way the entry guidelines exclude.
PowerShell scripts for auditing Secure Boot variables on Windows PCs. Desktop OS hardening, not embedded, same as sbctl and lanzaboote.
Generates and installs custom UEFI Secure Boot keys on desktop and laptop machines. Desktop OS hardening, not embedded.
Go library for Linux UEFI variables and Secure Boot signing, and the library underneath sbctl, which was declined for the same reason: the target is general-purpose machines, not embedded devices.
Chaos engineering platform for Kubernetes. Carries the fault-injection topic in the cloud-reliability sense, like istio, not glitching a chip.
Chaos engineering toolkit for cloud and container infrastructure. Same reason as chaos-mesh: fault injection in the reliability-testing sense.
Cloud-native chaos engineering for Kubernetes. Same reason as chaos-mesh.
Chaos testing and network emulation for Docker containers. Same reason as chaos-mesh.
Go library for injecting failures into code paths during testing. Software fault injection, not hardware.
Awesome list about testing distributed systems. Found through the fault-injection topic, but not an embedded security resource.
JavaScript library for visual glitch effects on web pages. Matched the glitching search on the word alone.
RISC-V processor core. Its debug module earns the jtag topic, but it is a CPU design, not a security tool.
Turns a photo of a key into a 3D-printable model. Physical lock bypass rather than embedded security.

Flipper Zero and ESP32 mods for Tesla vehicles, such as disabling driver-attention nags and unlocking FSD by region. Vehicle modding rather than a security research resource, and the repository has no license.
